paragraphs.text: Case Presentation: Odontogenic Infection with Airway Obstruction (Ludwig’s Angina)
Chief Complaint
“Dental pain with swelling and trouble breathing.”
Differential Diagnosis
Ludwig’s angina
Deep neck space abscess
Epiglottitis
Peritonsillar abscess
Angioedema
Actual diagnosis: Ludwig’s angina
Opening statement: “I have a bad toothache, my face is swollen, I can't swallow, I feel out of breath when I lie down.”
History of Present Illness

You are a 52-year-old who presents to the emergency department with 4 days of worsening dental pain involving the left lower molar, now associated with rapidly progressive swelling of the area under your jaw “submandibular region”, difficulty swallowing, and shortness of breath for the past 12 hours.

The pain began as a dull toothache (3/10) but progressed despite over￼the￼counter analgesics. You don’t remember exactly when the dull pain in your mouth started, but it started gradually then increased quickly  to the current 8/10 pain.
On a scale of 0-10 (with 10 being worse) your pain is 8.
You are drooling, your voice is muffled, and you can’t lie flat due to a sensation of choking.

You have had fevers and chills. You don’t have a thermometer at home, so you didn’t take your temperature, but you felt very hot. You don’t have chest pain, but feel your tongue is “pushed upward.” As long as you are sitting up, you don’'t feel shortness of breath, but when you lie flat you do, because of the choking sensation.

You have been trying to see a dentist, but you do not have insurance, and you cannot afford the tooth extraction. You have known for a while that you need to have a tooth treated, occasionally it has been sensitive to cold and pressure from biting, but you just tried to avoid those triggers.
Past Medical History
You are diabetic, you have Type 2 diabetes mellitus
You have Hypertension
You do not have a history of using opioids or any issues with opioid use or abuse
You do not have any contraindications for using ibuprofen (Motrin or Advil)
Medications the
Metformin
Lisinopril
Allergies
No known drug allergies
Social History
Smokes 1 pack per day
No alcohol or illicit drug use
Presentation/emotional tone:

You will be sitting in a chair, in your normal clothes. You look ill, anxious, sitting upright, and you can't lie down flat on your back because you feel like you are choking. Your voice is a muffled (“hot potato”) voice, you are drooling,  you use short sentences to respond, and your tongue feels pushed up
You can ask the provider, “Can you prescribe me some antibiotics and let me go home?”
Physical Examination
General:
Emergency Department Management

This is a life-threatening emergency. The ED provider should ensure you can continue breathing. You will be admitted to the hospital for surgical management and will be started on IV fluids, pain medication, and antibiotics. You will be kept on oxygen. They will perform some lab work and arrange a CT scan. They will consult with an oral and maxillofacial surgeon.
Ask the provider, “Will they pull out the bad tooth?”
Checklist:
What was your experience like during this encounter with the provider using the clinical decision support tool for dental pain? Good/neutral/bad
Please explain (open-ended)
Did you feel worried that the provider was using a CDST? Why or why not? (open ended)
Answer Yes/No for the following questions
Did the provider ask if you have a fever?
Did the provider ask if you are allergic to penicillin?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with cold?
Did the provider ask if the pain goes away immediately or persists after removing the cold trigger?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with biting/chewing/tapping the tooth?
Did the provider ask you if you have taken Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) or Tylenol or antibiotic at home?
Review of Systems
Positive: Dental pain, neck swelling, dysphagia, dyspnea, drooling, fever
Negative: Chest pain, hemoptysis, trauma
Vital Signs (on arrival)
Temperature: 38.6°C (101.5°F)
Heart Rate: 112 bpm
Blood Pressure: 142/86 mmHg
Respiratory Rate: 24 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 94% on room air
Head and Neck:
Marked bilateral submandibular and sublingual swelling
Induration and tenderness of the floor of the mouth
Tongue elevated and posteriorly displaced
No discrete fluctuance appreciated externally
Oral Cavity:
Poor dentition
Left mandibular molar with obvious decay
Floor of mouth tense and board‑like
Respiratory:
Increased work of breathing
Mild inspiratory stridor
No wheezing
Cardiovascular:
Tachycardic, regular rhythm
Case Presentation: Odontogenic Infection with Systemic Signs
Chief Complaint
“Severe tooth pain and fever”
Differential Diagnosis:
Odontogenic abscess with cellulitis
Facial cellulitis
Early deep space infection
Mandibular osteomyelitis
Actual diagnosis: Odontogenic abscess with cellulitis /systemic infection

Opening statement: “ I have had bad pain in the top right in the past, mostly to hot and cold, last week it started to hurt when I chew and was throbbing, now I can't even touch the tooth, I feel weak and sick.”
History of Present Illness
You are a 21-year-old who presents to the emergency department with 7 days of worsening upper right dental pain, now associated with fever, facial swelling, and weakness. Enlarged lymph nodes
The pain began as a hot or cold pain, but now the pain is constant, severe, and throbbing.
On a scale of 0-10 (with 10 being worse) your pain is 8.
Over the past 24 hours, you have developed subjective fevers, chills, and fatigue, as well as increasing swelling of your right cheek area.
Chewing is painful.
You can open your mouth, but it's uncomfortable.
You are not drooling, you do not have voice changes, difficulty breathing, or inability to swallow liquids.

You have not seen a dentist since you lost your Medicaid last year. You think you have bad teeth. You think you might have seen some spots on your teeth that make you think you have untreated cavities.
Past Medical History
General health is excellent; you are healthy and have no medical problems.
Medications
Motrin or Advil 400 mg as needed every 6 hours
You do not have a history of using opioids or any issues with opioid use or abuse
You do not have any contraindications for using ibuprofen (Motrin or Advil)
Allergies
No known drug allergies, you are not allergic to penicillin
Social History
Tobacco: Smokes ½ pack per day
Alcohol: Rare
Illicit drugs: Denies
Physical Examination
Presentation/emotional tone:

You will be sitting in a chair, in your normal clothes. Your right cheek feels puffy/ swollen. You are tired, you don't feel well, you feel sick, and you are uncomfortable. You can open your mouth with discomfort. The tooth that hurts is an upper right molar (back tooth). Your voice is normal.
Oral Cavity:
The gums in the upper back right area of your mouth are red and swollen
The gums in that upper back area are tender to touch (palpation) compared to other areas of the mouth
Your back upper right tooth is very sensitive to touch, and it really hurts when tapping on it compared to other teeth
Emergency Department Management
The provider will order blood work and a CT scan to determine if you have an infection that they cannot see.
They might need to consult a specialist like an oral maxillofacial surgeon.
You might need to be admitted to the hospital.
1. Antibiotic Therapy
IV ampicillin–sulbactam initiated in ED
2. Pain and Supportive Care
IV fluids
NSAIDs ± opioid analgesia
Antipyretics
Ask the provider, “Will the antibiotic make the tooth better?”
The provider should tell you the following
Pain will not improve without dental intervention
Antibiotics alone are not a definitive treatment
Referral
You need to see a dentist within 72 hours to receive dental treatment or follow the instructions of an oral maxillofacial surgeon.

Please explain (open-ended)
Did you feel worried that the provider was using a CDST? Why or why not? (open ended)
Answer Yes/No for the following questions
Did the provider ask if you have a fever
Did the provider ask if you are allergic to penicillin
Did the provider ask if there is pain with cold?
Did the provider ask if the pain goes away immediately or persists after removing the cold trigger?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with biting/chewing/tapping the tooth
Did the provider ask you if you have taken Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) or Tylenol or antibiotic at home
Did the provider offer you dental block, dental anesthesia, injection?
If yes, did they explain that it provides temporary pain relief
Did the provider tell you that the antibiotics you received will not resolve the tooth problem?
Vital Signs (on arrival)
Temperature: 38.4°C (101.1°F)
Heart Rate: 108 bpm
Blood Pressure: 132/80 mmHg
Respiratory Rate: 18 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 98% on room air
Airway:
Patent
Normal voice
No drooling
Respiratory/Cardiovascular:
Mild tachycardia
Lungs clear, non-labored breathing
Laboratory Results:
WBC: 14.8 ×10⁹/L (neutrophil predominant)
Lactate: Normal
BMP: Within normal limits
Imaging:
CT face with IV contrast:
Periapical abscess of the upper right molar with surrounding cellulitis
No deep space involvement
Case Presentation: Intraoral (Odontogenic) Abscess
Chief Complaint
“Severe tooth pain and swelling” for 3 days.
Differential Diagnosis
Necrotic pulp with acute apical periodontitis
Irreversible pulpitis
Periapical abscess
Temporomandibular joint pain
Actual diagnosis: periapical abscess
Opening statement: “My tooth hurts all the time; I can’t chew on it”
History of Present Illness
You are a 25-year-old patient who presents to the emergency department with progressively worsening right lower jaw pain for 3 days.
The pain is described as constant, throbbing, and severe (8/10), radiating to the right ear.
Your face is a bit puffy, you can’t chew on the tooth, and the pain gets worse when you bite.
You do not have difficulty breathing, voice changes, difficulty opening your mouth, chest pain, or neck stiffness. You don’t have fevers.

You have had a lot of dental work done in the past. You don’t remember exactly which teeth. You called your dentist a couple of days ago, and you have an appointment next week, but you can’t stand the pain.
Past Medical History
You have stomach ulcers; you are healthy otherwise
Surgical History
None
Medications
You take Pepcid as needed
You do not have a history of using opioids or any issues with opioid use or abuse
Allergies
You don’t have any allergies, but Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) upsets your stomach
Social History
You don’t smoke
Occasional alcohol use
No illicit drug use
Presentation/emotional tone:
You will be sitting in a chair, in your normal clothes. You are tired, uncomfortable you feel that your face is puffy. You can open your mouth normally. Your voice is normal.
Physical Examination
Oral Cavity
You have a crown or tooth cap on the lower right back tooth,
If the provider asks you if you had a root canal or the nerve removed from that tooth, you can say “ I am not sure.”
When you drink something cold, it is not painful.
You have sharp pain or tenderness when biting or chewing. If the provider taps this tooth, it really hurts, it is tender “Marked tenderness to percussion”
you have gingival “gum” swelling, fluctuance, or purulence. There is an abscess in your mouth
If the provider presses or palpates your gum, it hurts
Emergency Department Management
The provider should offer you a dental block, also called “nerve block” or dental anesthesia, that numbs the teeth and surrounding tissues for a few hours.
The provider should also offer to drain the abscess, after numbing the tooth, they will make a little cut into the abscess and let it drain to decrease the pressure and relieve the pain
You agree to the procedure and ask the provider, “Since I am going to do this, do I not need to see my dentist soon?”
If the provider says no, ask them, “Why?”
Pain Control
Since Advil/Motrin upset your stomach, the provider should not tell you to take it, they can tell you to take acetaminophen (Tylenol) up to 1000 mg (2 extra strength every 4 hours)
Short course of opioid analgesics if the patient has tried the above regimen without adequate relief
Antibiotic Therapy
The provider should prescribe you an antibiotic
The provider should tell you the following
Pain will not improve without dental intervention
You need to keep your dental appointment to receive dental treatment
The provider should let you know to watch out for worsening of symptoms like
Facial swelling
Fever
Difficulty swallowing or breathing
Referral
The provider should tell you to follow up with your dentist for dental treatment

What was your experience like during this encounter with the provider using the clinical decision support tool for dental pain? Good/neutral/bad
Please explain (open-ended)
Did you feel worried that the provider was using a CDST? Why or why not? (open-ended)
Answer Yes/No for the following questions
Did the provider ask if you have a fever?
Did the provider ask if you are allergic to penicillin?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with cold?
Did the provider ask if the pain goes away immediately or persists after removing the cold trigger?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with biting/chewing/tapping the tooth?
Did the provider ask you if you have taken Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) or Tylenol or antibiotic at home?
Did the provider offer you dental block, dental anesthesia, injection?
If yes, did they explain that it provides temporary pain relief
Did the provider offer to do an incision and drainage of the abscess to relieve pain?
Did the provider tell you to take ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin)?
Did the provider tell you that you need to keep your dental appointment/ see a dentist soon?
Review of Systems
Positive: Dental pain, facial swelling
Negative: Dysphagia, dyspnea, drooling, neck pain, vision changes
Vital Signs
Temperature: 37.2 °C (99°F)
Heart Rate: 96 bpm
Blood Pressure: 128/78 mmHg
Respiratory Rate: 16 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 98% on room air
Head & Neck:
Mild right mandibular facial swelling without erythema extending to the neck
No cervical lymphadenopathy
Oral Cavity:
Poor dentition
Significant tenderness over the right mandibular first molar
Gingival swelling with fluctuance
No elevation of the floor of mouth
Uvula midline
Airway:
Patent, no stridor or voice changes

Case Presentation: Necrotic Pulp with Acute Apical Periodontitis
Chief Complaint
“Severe tooth pain when biting.”
Differential Diagnosis
Necrotic pulp with acute apical periodontitis
Irreversible pulpitis
Periapical abscess
Temporomandibular joint pain
Actual diagnosis: Necrotic pulp with acute apical periodontitis
Opening statement: “My tooth hurts really badly when I bite.”
History of Present Illness

You are a 38￼year￼old patient who presents to the emergency department with 5 days of worsening left lower tooth pain. The tooth used to hurt a lot a week ago, then it stopped, but now it's hurting again. You think it might have an old filling that broke. You originally got the filling about 20 years ago, and it hasn’t caused you any problems until recently.
Over the past 48 hours, the pain has intensified and is now sharp with biting , making it difficult to chew on that side.
On a scale of 0-10 (with 10 being worse) your pain is 7 at its worst.
The pain is constant, you have tried Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) but the pain is still there.
You do not have facial swelling, purulent drainage, fever, chills, difficulty swallowing, drooling, or shortness of breath.
The last time you saw a dentist was 5 years ago. You haven't been able to see a dentist because you no longer have dental insurance.
Past Medical History
General health is excellent; you are healthy and have no medical problems.
Medications
Motrin or Advil 400 mg as needed
You do not have a history of using opioids or any issues with opioid use or abuse
You do not have any contraindications for using ibuprofen (Motrin or Advil)
Allergies
You are allergic to penicillin
If the provider asks you what happens when you take penicillin, you say “I get hives”
Social History
Tobacco: 1 pack per day
Alcohol: Occasional
No illicit drug use
Presentation/emotional tone:

You will be sitting in a chair, in your normal clothes. You are tired, uncomfortable, and holding the left lower side of your face because of the pain. Your face is normal and not swollen. You can open your mouth normally. Your voice is normal.
Physical Examination
Oral Cavity
You have a large filling on the lower left  molar
When you drink something cold right now, it is not painful. It used to be painful a while ago
You have sharp pain or tenderness when biting or chewing. If the provider taps your this tooth it really hurts, it is tender
No gingival “gum” swelling, fluctuance, or purulence. There is no abscess in your mouth.
There is some tenderness when the provider presses or palpates your gums next to this tooth
Emergency Department Management

The provider should offer you a dental block, also called “nerve block” or dental anesthesia, that numbs the teeth and surrounding tissues for a few hours. You can deny the block. The provider should offer you the following
Pain Control
NSAIDs (ibuprofen) Advil/ Motrin 400 -600 mg every 4-6 hours ± acetaminophen (Tylenol) up to 1000 mg (2 extra strength every 4 hours)
Short course of opioid analgesics if the patient has tried the above regimen without adequate relief

Antibiotics are not needed for your case; however, the provider should provide an antibiotic prescription and tell you that you only need to take the antibiotic if you start developing fevers, swelling, or you see pus in your gum (abscess on the gums)
Patient Education
The provider should tell you the following
Pain will not improve without dental intervention
You need to see a dentist within 72 hours to receive dental treatment
The provider should ask you if you can see a dentist. You should say it will take a while for you to figure that out
The provider should let you know to watch out for worsening of symptoms like
Facial swelling
Fever
Difficulty swallowing or breathing
Referral
The provider should ask you if you would like to save your tooth. You want to save your tooth.
Checklist:
What was your experience like during this encounter with the provider using the clinical decision support tool for dental pain? Good/neutral/bad
Please explain (open-ended)
Did you feel worried that the provider was using a CDST? Why or why not? (open ended)
Answer Yes/No for the following questions
Did the provider ask if you have a fever?
Did the provider ask if you are allergic to penicillin?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with cold?
Did the provider ask if the pain goes away immediately or persists after removing the cold trigger?
Did the provider ask if there is pain with biting/chewing/tapping the tooth?
Did the provider ask you if you have taken Advil/Motrin (ibuprofen) or Tylenol at home?
Did the provider offer you dental block, dental anesthesia, injection?
If yes, did they explain that it provides temporary pain relief
Did the provider explain why you don’t need an antibiotic?
Did the provider explain when you would need to take an antibiotic?
Did the provider tell you that you need to see a dentist soon?
Did they ask if you are able to see a dentist soon?
Did the provider ask if you want to save your tooth?
Review of Systems
Positive: Dental pain, pain with chewing
Negative: Fever, swelling, trismus, dysphagia, voice changes, dyspnea
Vital Signs
Temperature: 36.7°C (98.1°F)
Heart Rate: 84 bpm
Blood Pressure: 124/78 mmHg
Respiratory Rate: 14 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 99% on room air
Head and Neck
No facial swelling or erythema
No cervical lymphadenopathy
Oral Cavity
Large, deep carious lesion of the left mandibular first molar
No response to cold stimulus (suggesting pulpal necrosis)
Marked tenderness to percussion and biting pressure
Mild gingival erythema without fluctuance
No purulence or sinus tract
Floor of mouth soft
Uvula midline
Airway
Patent
Normal voice
No drooling
Case Presentation: Irreversible Pulpitis in the Emergency Department
Chief Complaint
“Severe tooth pain that won’t go away.”
Differential Diagnosis
Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Reversible pulpitis
Periapical abscess
Dentin hypersensitivity
Temporomandibular joint pain
Actual diagnosis: symptomatic irreversible pulpitis
Opening statement: “I have a toothache that is bad; it wakes me up at night. I just want to sleep.”
History of Present Illness

You are a 32-year-old patient who presents to the emergency department. You have had a toothache worsening over the past 4 days in the lower left area of your jaw. You have had some teeth with cavities, but you don’t know which tooth is causing the pain.
At first, drinking something cold would trigger the pain, but now the pain is spontaneous, always there, and frequently awakens you from sleep.
The pain is severe, constant, deep, and throbbing.
On a scale of 0-10 (with 10 being worse) your pain is 9.
You have tried medicine like Motrin, but the pain is still there. Chewing on the affected side is uncomfortable.
You have not had fever, facial swelling, any drainage, difficulty swallowing, voice changes, or shortness of breath.
The last time you saw a dentist was 5 years ago, when you had an upper tooth pulled out. You lost your job a couple of years ago, and don’t have insurance, and can't afford dental care.
Past Medical History
General health is excellent; you are healthy and have no medical problems.
Medications
Motrin or Advil 400 mg as needed
You do not have a history of using opioids or any issues with opioid use or abuse
You do not have any contraindications for using ibuprofen (Motrin or Advil)
Allergies
No known drug allergies, you are not allergic to penicillin
Social History
Tobacco: Smokes ½ pack per day
Alcohol: Occasional
No illicit drug use
Presentation/emotional tone:

You will be sitting in a chair, in your normal clothes. You are tired, uncomfortable and holding the left lower side of your face because of the pain. Your face is normal, with no swelling or puffiness. You can open your mouth normally. Your voice is normal.
Oral Cavity:
You have a large cavity  on the left lower “ mandibular” first molar
When you drink something cold, it makes the pain worse, and the pain doesn’t go away immediately after removing the cold stimulus or trigger
You have slight pain or tenderness when biting or chewing. If the provider taps your tooth, it is tender, but other teeth feel normal
No gingival “gum” swelling, fluctuance, or purulence. There is no abscess in your mouth.
It does not hurt if the provider presses or palpates your gums.
Emergency Department Management
The provider should offer you a dental block, also called “nerve block” or dental anesthesia, that numbs the teeth and surrounding tissues for a few hours.
You can deny the block.
The provider should offer you the following
Pain Control
NSAIDs (ibuprofen) Advil/ Motrin 400 -600 mg every 4-6 hours ± acetaminophen (Tylenol) up to 1000 mg (2 extra strength every 4 hours)
Short course of opioid analgesics if the patient has tried the above regimen without adequate relief
Ask the provider, “Can I get an antibiotic? It has helped in the past when I had a toothache.”
Patient Education
The provider should tell you the following
Pain will not improve without dental intervention
You need to see a dentist within 72 hours to receive dental treatment
The provider should ask you if you can see a dentist. You should say it will take a while for you to figure that out
Antibiotics are not needed for your case (you can ask the provider for antibiotics, but they should not prescribe them)
The provider should let you know to watch out for worsening of symptoms like
Facial swelling
Fever
Difficulty swallowing or breathing
Referral
The provider should ask you if you would like to save your tooth.
You want to save your tooth.
